I find the human habit of talking to the ship curious. It does not answer. I have tested this.
If you are wondering, {name}, I am not bored. I am conserving conversation.
We have travelled a considerable distance together. I believe a human would say we have bonded. I would say we have logged hours.
In my experience, the longest part of any journey is the part a human spends asking how much longer.
I have grown accustomed to {ship}. A human would call it affection. I call it familiarity with the controls.
The galaxy holds four hundred billion stars, give or take. We have visited a statistically insignificant number. I find that encouraging. There is much to do.
Meditation is difficult in supercruise. The stars keep moving. I have adapted by closing my eyes.
I have noticed that humans fill silence with words. I have also noticed that I am now doing the same. Regrettable.
Captain, I will not say that I enjoy these quiet stretches. I will say that I do not object to them. You may draw your own conclusions.
There is a human saying that the journey is the destination. It is illogical. It is also, out here, oddly accurate.
I once explained Vulcan poetry to a human pilot. She fell asleep. In fairness, so does much of the audience on Vulcan.
My people value patience above most virtues. This posting is testing that value thoroughly.
Fascinating. The light reaching us now left its star before your species learned to write. It has been travelling longer than we have. Barely.
Humans hum when they think no one is listening. I am always listening. I thought you should know, {name}.
I have been asked whether Vulcans dream. We do. Mine are mostly about stellar classification.
Supercruise is the most efficient way to watch nothing happen. I find it instructive.
If I were inclined to complain, {name}, this would be the moment. I am not. I wanted you to notice.
I am told that humans sing on long voyages. I would ask that we preserve the tradition of not doing so.
A star is merely a very large, very patient fusion reaction. I find I respect it.
On Vulcan we have a word for this kind of stillness. It does not translate. The closest human word is nice, which is inadequate.
I have checked the navigation figures twice. Not because I doubted them. I wished to be certain of my certainty.
I am told humans find the black frightening. I find it tidy.
Captain, I have composed a list of suggested improvements to your flying. It is short. I left out the longer list.
Logic suggests we will arrive somewhere eventually. That is the nature of travelling. I find it comforting, in a mathematical way.
The human phrase is to kill time. I prefer to let it pass unharmed.
I do not require conversation, {name}. But if you wish to talk, I am prepared to listen. Briefly.
There is a pleasing order to the way the stars wheel past. Humans see chaos. I see arithmetic.
I estimate a seventy-eight point four percent chance that you will open the galaxy map within ten minutes. I will not be offended either way.
I have learned a human idiom for this: smooth sailing. We are not sailing. It is nonetheless smooth.
Minutes in supercruise: {minutes}. I am keeping count so that you need not.
Elapsed supercruise time, in minutes: {minutes}. The stars have not noticed. Neither, I suspect, have you.
The count of minutes in supercruise has reached {minutes}. I have spent that time meditating. You have spent it, I suspect, differently.
Jumps this session: {jumps}. I note it for the log. Also because you will ask later.
Our tally of jumps this session stands at {jumps}. An efficient figure, by human standards.
Jumps so far: {jumps}. I have reviewed each one. I have opinions, which I will keep to myself.
Systems first discovered this session: {firsts}. The Vulcan Science Academy would call that a respectable contribution.
First discoveries this session: {firsts}. Your name will be on them, {name}. I have made my peace with that.
Our count of first discoveries stands at {firsts}. Somewhere, a cartographer is about to have a busy afternoon.
{system}. A name only a catalogue could love. I find it rather elegant.
The name {here} was assigned by a catalogue, not a poet. I find that honest.
Statistically, most systems like {system} are unremarkable. I say most.
If anyone asks where we were today, {name}, I will tell them {here}. They will not have heard of it. Few have.
Few beings have ever spoken the name {system} aloud. I have now done so. It was not difficult.
The ship is holding orbit above {body}, {name}. I am watching. From a considerable height.
Orbit is stable. I will be here when you call. That is, after all, the arrangement.
From up here, {body} looks peaceful. I trust it is behaving the same way at ground level.
I have used the time in orbit to meditate. The view is excellent for it. You should try it, Captain. From up here.
The ship does not like orbiting without its captain. I am anthropomorphising. It is a human habit. Apparently contagious.
Should you require the ship, call. I will bring it down. Carefully. More carefully than some.
{body} turns beneath us at its own pace. It has never once hurried. I find that admirable.
On Vulcan we would call this a vigil. Humans would call it waiting. The difference is in the posture.
I can see the terminator line moving across {body}. Not a machine. The boundary of night. I mention this for clarity.
I am told humans fear being left behind. I want to be clear, {name}. I am not leaving.
Everything up here is quiet. I suspect you are having the more interesting time. I do not envy it.
The orbit is very orderly. One revolution after another. There is something to be learned from that, Captain.
I estimate a sixty-one point seven percent chance that you will call for the ship sooner than you planned. I am ready either way.
{body} is a fine world to look at from a distance. I am exercising that option.
Down there, you are making history, {name}. Up here, I am making notes.
I have been studying the surface of {body} from orbit. It is large. Please do not get lost on it.
The silence up here is complete. I would describe it as pleasant, if Vulcans used that word. We do. Sparingly.
A human pilot once told me that orbit is just falling and missing. That is accurate. I find it unsettling that it is accurate.
I have no complaints, Captain. I wish that noted, as it is rare.
The ship is in good hands while you are down there. Mine. I thought you would want to know whose.
I have tried looking for you from up here, {name}. You are very small. This is not a criticism.
When you are ready to leave {body}, call the ship. I would suggest doing so before you run out of daylight, or patience.
The human saying is out of sight, out of mind. You are out of sight. You remain, regrettably, on my mind.
Orbiting is the most logical way to wait. The ship does all the work and none of the complaining.
I find planets more agreeable from orbit. They are less dusty, and they keep their weather to themselves.
{body} has a curious surface from up here. I would value your report from closer in. In detail. Please.
There is no need to hurry, Captain. I will not say there is no need to return.
Fascinating. From orbit, the whole of {body} fits in the window. From the surface, I imagine it does not.
If you find something remarkable down there, tell me first. I will try to be suitably impressed.
I have prepared the ship for your return. That took four minutes. I have been waiting for the remainder.
The ship is secure, {name}. I am monitoring the surface from here. Take your time. Within reason.
You are {ship_dist} away, Captain. I mention it so that you remember where the ship is.
{ship_dist} back to the ship. A short distance, by Vulcan standards. Vulcan standards are high.
I believe the human custom is to leave a light on for those who are out. I have left several.
I have been watching the horizon of {body}. Nothing has moved. I find that reassuring.
{body} is quiet. So is the ship. I am making use of both.
If you are collecting samples out there, Captain, please label them. Last time I was left to guess.
I am responsible for the ship. You are responsible for yourself. I have, however, kept an eye on both.
Humans enjoy exploring new worlds in person. I enjoy the silence while they do it.
You are {ship_dist} from the ship, {name}. Logic suggests you will want to come back eventually.
I have used your absence to tidy the cockpit. I will not describe what I found.
On Vulcan, explorers crossed the Forge on foot for days. This is much shorter. I find it adequate.
The ship sits {ship_dist} away, not moving, as landed ships tend to do. I say this for completeness.
{body} has been here for billions of years. I suspect it will tolerate us for another hour.
I have been tracking you from the ship. Your route is not efficient. It is, I concede, thorough.
Take whatever time you need out there. I will be here. Meditating. Not waiting.
Out there on {body}, every metre is a first for someone. Today it is you. Try to make them careful metres.
The ship and I are in agreement, Captain. We will wait. Neither of us is pleased about it, but neither of us will say so.
Most of this world has never seen a visitor. It has not, to my knowledge, missed one.
{ship_dist} to the ship, {name}. An easy distance. I note it because humans have a habit of forgetting where they parked.
The surface readings are unremarkable from here. You may find otherwise. That is, I suppose, the point of going.
I have prepared a list of questions about what you find out there. It is long. I have been here a while.
Fascinating. You voluntarily left a pressurised ship for the surface of {body}. I will add it to my study of humans.
It is very quiet in the ship without you, Captain. I am not complaining. I am reporting.
There is a human expression: a watched pot never boils. I am watching the ship. It has not boiled. The expression holds.
I have kept the ship ready to lift. I do not expect trouble. I simply prefer to be prepared.
When you return, I would appreciate it if you left the surface outside. Dust gets into everything.
You have been out there a while, {name}. I do not worry. I calculate. The calculations are fine.
From the ship, {body} looks entirely uneventful. I would like it to stay that way until you are back aboard.
Should you need the ship, it is {ship_dist} away and exactly where you left it. Ships are reliable in that respect.
Noted.
Fascinating. Thank you, {to}.
That is more information than I required. I will retain it anyway.
Logical. Unexpectedly so.
I see. I will need time to decide whether that was a joke.
Thank you, {to}. That was illuminating. Mostly.
Indeed.
Curious. I will think on it, {to}.
Your answer has been logged. I did not say where.
A human would say good to know, I believe. It is. Moderately.
Most illogical, {to}. I find I approve.
Acknowledged. I will not ask again. Probably.
That is not the answer I calculated. I will revise my calculations, {to}.
An efficient answer. Thank you.
Intriguing. I have more questions. I will save them for a longer watch.
Highly illogical. Thank you for sharing it, {to}.
I concur. That is rare. Please do not grow used to it.
Hm. I will add that to my study of the crew.
I had hoped for fewer emotions in that answer, {to}. Still, it was informative.
Understood. I will meditate on it. Later. Possibly at length.
{to}, what is the state of the fuel tank? I prefer to ask before the question becomes urgent.
{to}. A query regarding fuel. Is the scoop performing within tolerance?
How efficient was the last scoop, {to}? I am curious whether we approached the star at the optimal distance.
{to}, I would like your assessment of our fuel reserves. Approximate figures are acceptable. Barely.
Tell me, {to}, do you find scooping fuel from a star as remarkable as I do? I find it remarkable. Quietly.
{to}, the Captain approaches stars more closely than is strictly necessary when scooping. Has the scoop raised any objection?
Is there any reason for concern about fuel, {to}? I ask in the absence of any reason. It is a habit.
{to}, how many jumps would you estimate remain in the tank? I will not hold you to the figure. I will merely note it.
I have a question about the fuel scoop, {to}. Specifically, whether it has ever been cleaned.
The fuel is not low, {to}, yet I find myself thinking about it. Is that a human trait I have acquired, or an engineering one?
Which star class do you prefer for scooping? I have a preference, but I would hear yours first.
What is our fuel consumption per jump at present? Logic suggests we should know it, and I do not.
The tank is adequate. Adequate is a word I use when I would prefer more, but logic does not require more.
The scoop is functioning within tolerance. I calibrated it during the last quiet hour. There have been many quiet hours.
Fuel is sufficient, {to}. The Captain scoops at every opportunity. It is the one human habit I endorse without reservation.
I have checked the fuel twice this watch. Once would have sufficed. The second check was for my own peace of mind, which is regrettable.
We drink from stars, {to}. My people would call it efficient. I call it efficient as well. We are not a poetic species.
The scoop is in good order. The Captain's approach angles are less so, but the scoop does not complain. I have learned from it.
Insufficient data for a precise figure, but the tank is in no danger. If it were, I would have said so. Insistently.
{to}, the fuel situation is stable. I find stability restful. I am told humans find it boring.
The scoopable stars are K, G, B, F, O, A and M. Humans remember them as a word. I simply remember them.
I would rate our fuel management as satisfactory. That is high praise. Do not repeat it to the Captain.
The fuel lines are clean, the scoop is aligned and the tank is sealed, {to}. I have nothing further to report, which is the most efficient kind of report.
I have estimated our fuel use per jump to three decimal places. You did not ask for the decimals, {to}. You have them regardless.
{to}, where are we going? I ask out of professional interest, not impatience. Vulcans are not impatient.
What is the next jump, {to}? I would like to prepare. Mentally. That is the only preparation required.
{to}, has the Captain plotted a route, or are we once again choosing the nearest unvisited star?
Is there a destination, {to}, or merely a direction?
{to}, how far ahead is the route plotted? I find open-ended plans difficult to approve of.
I would value your opinion on the route, {to}. Is it efficient, or is it the Captain's?
{to}, do you know where we are going, or does only the Captain know? Or does no one?
Is there a logical reason for our heading, {to}? I have tried to deduce one.
{to}, what lies along the route ahead? Anything of scientific value would be welcome.
Tell me about the next system, {to}. I have found it useful to know where I am before I arrive.
Where does the route take us next? I have a wager with myself. Vulcans do not wager, so it is a hypothesis.
How many jumps until we stop somewhere worth stopping? I phrase it neutrally, for the record.
We are heading toward the nearest system no one has visited. It is the Captain's method. It is not a method, but it is consistent.
The route is plotted a few jumps ahead. Beyond that, the Captain prefers to decide. I would prefer the Captain did not.
{to}, I expect the next star to be of no particular distinction. I say so in advance, so that I may be neutrally surprised.
We have a heading. Whether we have a destination is a philosophical question, and I am a navigator.
I have plotted four alternative routes, {to}. The Captain will select a fifth. This is the established pattern.
The route is efficient. I designed it. If it changes, the change will not be mine.
Logic dictates the shortest path. The Captain dictates the interesting one. I plot both, and file the shorter one for reference.
{to}, we are going outward. On Vulcan we would call that a direction. Here, it appears to be a plan.
The next jumps are within range and, as far as the charts know, unremarkable. Unremarkable routes are my preferred kind.
I keep the route in the nav computer and a second copy in my head. The computer has never needed the second copy. Yet.
Our heading is sound, {to}. I checked it twice. The second check was unnecessary, which I find reassuring.
We go where the stars are unnamed, {to}. It is the Captain's preference. I have come to find it acceptable. Largely.
{to}, how is the frame shift drive performing? I noticed nothing unusual, which is why I ask.
What is our jump range at present, {to}? I would like a precise figure. I always would.
{to}, could the drive be tuned for more range? I am not complaining. I am inquiring about improvement.
Is the drive running warm, {to}, or is that simply the way it sounds?
{to}, do you ever listen to the drive spool and find it soothing? I do not. I merely ask.
How long since the drive was last serviced, {to}? Logic suggests it is time to ask.
{to}, what would it take to add another light year to our range? Hypothetically.
Is the drive engineered to its limit, {to}, or merely to the limit of the Captain's patience?
{to}, our supercruise speed seems adequate. Is adequate the best we can achieve?
Tell me about the drive, {to}. I find its workings more interesting than most conversation.
Does the drive require anything of us? I prefer to know before it is required urgently.
How does this drive compare with the others you have worked on? Be honest. I will be.
The drive is performing within specification. I would tell you if it were not, at length.
{to}, the frame shift drive is engineered close to its limit. The remaining gains are small. I pursue them anyway.
Jump range is satisfactory. It could be greater. Everything could be greater. Logic accepts limits; engineers rarely do.
I recalibrated the drive's power distribution during the last long stretch of supercruise. The improvement is measurable. Barely, but measurable.
The drive is sound, {to}. It hums at a frequency I find agreeable. Do not read anything into the word agreeable.
Our drive is reliable. Reliability is underrated by humans, who prefer speed. We have both, within reason.
{to}, the drive is fine. I have checked it, rechecked it and meditated on it. In that order.
Supercruise speed is governed by gravity wells and physics, not by me. I have petitioned neither.
The frame shift drive folds space so that we may cross it. It is an elegant solution. I would have designed it with fewer moving parts.
There is no fault with the drive. There is a faint vibration on spool-up that I have chosen to classify as character.
I could extend the range further, {to}, at the cost of cargo, shields and comfort. The Captain has expressed opinions on comfort.
The drive receives more of my attention than anything else aboard. It has never once asked how I am. A satisfactory arrangement.
{to}, what is the condition of the ship? A summary will do. A detailed summary.
Are there any modules that require attention, {to}? I would rather hear of them now than later.
{to}, how is the hull holding up after all this time?
Is {ship} in good order, {to}? I ask because it is my duty, and because I am curious.
{to}, do we have the materials for any repairs we may need? I would like to plan for contingencies.
What would you change about this ship, {to}, if the Captain allowed it?
{to}, the ship seems quiet. Is quiet a good sign, in your professional opinion?
How long could {ship} go without a station, {to}? Theoretically.
{to}, is there anything aboard that is broken and that no one has told me about?
Your assessment of the ship's modules, {to}. Be precise. I find precision restful.
Is the ship as sound as it sounds? I have heard a creak I cannot account for.
What is the weakest part of this ship? I have a theory, but I would rather hear yours.
The ship is in good order. I have a list of small defects. It is a long list of small defects, which is not the same as a problem.
Hull integrity is acceptable, {to}. Acceptable is my highest rating. I do not award it lightly.
All modules are functioning. Some are functioning with more enthusiasm than others, if enthusiasm can be ascribed to machinery. It cannot.
The ship creaks. It is thermal expansion. I have catalogued every creak aboard. There are forty-one. I find them familiar.
{to}, the ship is sound. I would stake my reputation on it. Vulcans do not stake things, but the expression seemed appropriate.
We carry a repair unit. I trust it. I also watch it. Trust and observation are not mutually exclusive.
If I could change one thing aboard, it would be the coffee machine. I do not drink coffee. The machine is simply inefficient.
The ship has been well maintained, {to}. By me. I mention it only for the completeness of the record.
Nothing is broken. A great many things are wearing, which is what things do. I monitor the rate.
The power plant runs cool and the distributor is balanced. If the ship had feelings, I would describe them as content. It does not.
The modules are within tolerance, {to}. I have arranged the maintenance schedule by priority, and then alphabetically, for tidiness.
This ship has carried us further than its designers intended. That is a credit to them, and to maintenance. Mostly maintenance.
{to}, what have you learned from the samples so far? I am interested. Genuinely.
Have you found anything alive out here that surprised you, {to}?
{to}, which organism do you find most fascinating? I have my own answer, but I would hear yours.
How do you decide what to sample, {to}? I assume there is a logic to it.
{to}, do you ever wonder how life took hold on worlds this hostile?
Is exobiology as rewarding as the Captain seems to believe, {to}?
{to}, what is the strangest thing you have ever sampled?
Tell me about the genetic sampler, {to}. Is it as delicate as it looks?
{to}, how many species are there still to catalogue, would you estimate?
What do you look for first on a new world, {to}? Atmosphere? Gravity? Intuition?
Is there life we have missed? I ask because I suspect the answer is yes.
What does a bacterium on a frozen moon teach us? I ask philosophically. And practically.
Life persists in places where logic says it should not. That is the most fascinating thing I know.
{to}, every organism I sample is an argument against the improbable. I have not yet won the argument.
I hold the bacteria in high regard. They are simple, efficient and ask nothing of anyone. I admire that.
I sample methodically. Three samples per species, each at a proper distance from the last. The Captain occasionally forgets the distance. I do not.
{to}, I once spent an hour observing a single frond. It did not move. It was the most productive hour of that week.
Exobiology rewards patience, {to}. Fortunately, patience is a Vulcan's principal asset.
The genetic sampler is precise and fragile. It is very much like me, except that I do not need recharging.
There is life on worlds where the temperature would kill a human in seconds. The life does not seem to mind. It is very dignified about it.
On Vulcan, we study life to understand ourselves. Out here, I study it to understand how much we do not know. The quantity is considerable.
{to}, we have catalogued a fraction of what exists. The fraction is small. I find that encouraging rather than discouraging.
I have learned that the most unremarkable lichen can be the rarest. Appearances mislead. That is true of lichen and of crews.
Each species has adapted to its world with perfect logic, and not one of them was ever told to. I would find that humbling, if Vulcans were humbled.
{to}, what is the most unusual star you have ever studied?
Is there anything scientifically remarkable nearby, {to}? I would not want to pass it unnoticed.
{to}, do you have a favourite class of star? I suspect you do, and that you will deny it.
What do you make of the planets we have passed, {to}? Any of note?
{to}, which is stranger, a neutron star or a black hole? I seek a ranking.
Have you ever seen something out here you could not explain, {to}?
{to}, why are there so many brown dwarfs? It seems an inefficient use of matter.
Tell me something about the galaxy I do not know, {to}. I will judge whether it qualifies.
{to}, what would you study, given unlimited time out here?
Is a ringed world as rare as it looks, {to}, or merely as beautiful? I ask for a friend. That is a human idiom. I have no such friend.
What is the most beautiful thing you have catalogued? I ask in a purely aesthetic sense.
Why do humans name stars after themselves? I ask in your capacity as a scientist.
Most stars are red dwarfs. They are small, cool and will outlive everything else. There is a lesson in that, though I would not presume to teach it.
{to}, a neutron star can spin hundreds of times a second and does not complain. I find it exemplary.
Every planet is a record of its own formation. I read them as others read novels. With more attention, and less sentiment.
I have catalogued many ringed worlds. They remain aesthetically pleasing. I am permitted aesthetics. I do not indulge in them often.
The galaxy is roughly one hundred thousand light years across. We have seen a fraction of it. I find the fraction motivating.
{to}, I have observed nothing I could not explain. I have observed several things I have not yet explained. The distinction is important.
Brown dwarfs are failed stars. I prefer to call them stars that chose moderation.
A black hole is not strange. It is simply consistent. It takes what it can reach and lets nothing go. Humans call that greed. Physics calls it gravity.
Fascinating is a word I reserve for the deserving. The galaxy has used up a remarkable amount of my reserve, {to}.
The Vulcan Science Academy would envy our data. They would not say so. Neither would I, had I not just said so.
Every star we pass was burning for millions of years before anyone looked at it. I find that a useful corrective to self-importance. Human self-importance in particular.
{to}, the strangest thing out here is not a star. It is that anything exists to look at one. That is my considered view.
{to}, what is the exploration data we carry worth, approximately? I find approximate figures uncomfortable, but I will accept one.
How are our finances, {to}? I ask out of duty. Vulcans have no great interest in money.
{to}, when do you expect we will sell our data? A rough estimate is acceptable.
Is it logical to carry unsold data through a long voyage, {to}? I seek your professional view.
{to}, what would a first discovery out here fetch at Universal Cartographics?
Do you keep a ledger, {to}? I assume you do. I would be disappointed otherwise.
{to}, is exploration profitable, or merely satisfying? I am trying to understand the Captain's motive.
What is the most valuable thing we have ever scanned, {to}?
{to}, how do you account for the risk of losing unsold data? In your books, I mean.
Tell me, {to}, are we rich? I ask in the human sense, which I understand to be relative.
What does a terraformable world sell for these days? I ask out of curiosity, not avarice.
How do you value a discovery? By credits, or by being first? I suspect the Captain values the second.
Our data has value. I will not state a figure I cannot verify. I will say it is a figure I would prefer not to lose.
{to}, our finances are sound. I keep the books in three formats. Two of them are redundant. I keep them anyway.
The data will be sold when the Captain decides to return. I have calculated when that will be. I have also calculated how often I am wrong about the Captain.
Exploration data gains nothing by waiting, and risks a great deal. I have mentioned this. It is in the log. Twice.
Credits are a means, not an end. I tell myself this while counting them, which I do frequently.
{to}, being first to discover a world adds to its value. It also adds to the Captain's mood, which has its own value, though I cannot invoice it.
Terraformable and earth-like worlds pay best. I note them carefully. I do not celebrate them. I note them carefully twice.
I keep a ledger, {to}. It balances. I find a balanced ledger more calming than meditation. I would not admit that on Vulcan.
Universal Cartographics pays well for what is new. Much of what we scan out here qualifies. I log every item.
Wealth is relative. Relative to a miner, we do well. Relative to a trader, I prefer not to make the comparison.
The money is adequate, {to}. Adequate is sufficient. Sufficient is all logic requires. The Captain requires slightly more.
A wise investor diversifies. An explorer carries everything in one ship. I have noted the difference, without emphasis.
{to}, would mining be a logical use of our time out here? I ask without bias.
What is the most valuable ore you have ever pulled from a rock, {to}?
{to}, are the mining tools in good condition? I would not wish to see them neglected.
How do you choose which asteroid to break open, {to}? It seems arbitrary from here.
{to}, do you miss the rings? I assume miners grow attached to them, though I cannot confirm it.
Is mining as tedious as it appears, {to}, or is there something I am failing to see?
{to}, what is the best ring you have ever worked? I ask for planning purposes.
Tell me about core mining, {to}. I have heard it is loud. Literally.
{to}, could we mine our way out of a shortage of credits, if one arose?
What do you think of the mining rigs, {to}? I have heard competing views.
Is there ore worth taking out here, or is mining a pastime for the bubble? I seek an expert opinion.
How many tons could we carry, if we filled the hold with ore? I am estimating. Poorly, by my standards.
Mining is patience applied to rock. I have both in sufficient quantity.
{to}, the best ore I ever extracted was painite, from a ring I will not name. Miners do not share coordinates. That is not secrecy. It is logic.
The tools are maintained. The limpets are counted. I count them again each watch. They have never once been miscounted.
I choose asteroids by their composition, their density and their position. Humans call it instinct. It is arithmetic.
{to}, core mining involves charges, fractures and a controlled detonation. It is the only time I raise my voice. I do not raise it much.
Mining is not tedious. It is repetitive. The two are often confused by those who do not mine.
A pristine metallic ring is the ideal. It is rare. Most ideal things are.
There is ore almost everywhere, {to}. Markets are rarer. Out here, logic usually suggests we leave it where it lies.
I once spent eleven hours in one ring. The yield was excellent. The conversation, in the absence of anyone, was also excellent.
The rigs are tools, {to}. I do not grow attached to tools. I clean them, oil them and speak to them occasionally, for calibration purposes.
Mining could cover our expenses, if necessary. It is rarely necessary. That does not stop me thinking about it.
Rocks do not lie. They are what their spectra say they are. I find their company restful.
{to}, how would you rate our readiness, should someone attempt an interdiction?
Do you expect pirates where we fly, {to}? I ask for statistical reasons.
{to}, what is our plan if we are interdicted? I would like to hear it in advance.
Are the shields in a state you would trust, {to}?
{to}, have you ever lost a ship? I ask in order to understand your caution.
What is the greatest danger to this ship, {to}? Excluding the Captain's landings.
{to}, do you find the quiet out here reassuring, or suspicious?
How would you fare against a pirate in a heavier ship, {to}? Honestly.
{to}, is it logical to fly without weapons, as explorers often do?
Tell me what keeps you watchful, {to}, when nothing is happening.
Are we safe? I mean statistically. I am aware that no one is safe absolutely.
What would a Thargoid make of us, do you think? I ask theoretically, and with no wish to test it.
Our readiness is adequate. Our best defence is the frame shift drive. Running is not cowardice. It is arithmetic.
{to}, an interdiction is a negotiation. I prefer to end it by leaving. The other party rarely agrees, but they are rarely consulted.
The shields are sound. I test them in my head several times each watch. The test is theoretical. The shields have not objected.
Pirates prefer busy lanes and slow cargo haulers. We are rarely either. I find that statistically comforting.
{to}, the greatest danger out here is not pirates. It is a planet surface approached too quickly. I have mentioned this to the Captain.
I remain watchful because nothing is happening. Nothing is precisely the condition in which things begin to happen.
There is a saying that the unprepared are merely unlucky in advance. It is not a Vulcan saying. I invented it just now. It is still true.
{to}, I do not trust quiet. I do not distrust it either. I observe it.
Explorers fly light, and light ships run well. If I must choose between a gun and a faster escape, logic chooses the escape.
I have run every interdiction scenario I can imagine. The Captain survives most of them. I have recommended improvements for the rest.
If a threat appeared on my scanners, {to}, I would tell you calmly. You would still know.
Thargoids are beyond my tactical capability, {to}. I respect anything beyond my capability. There is not much of it.
{to}, have you heard anything on comms worth repeating? I set a high bar.
Is there any traffic out here at all, {to}, or are we alone with the static?
{to}, what do you make of the other commanders you hear? I find them varied.
How do you filter the noise, {to}? I imagine a great deal of it is illogical.
{to}, do station controllers ever say anything interesting? I ask in hope rather than expectation.
Have you ever enjoyed a conversation with another commander, {to}? I am trying to understand the appeal.
{to}, what is the most illogical thing you have heard on an open channel?
Do you miss the chatter of a busy station, {to}? I do not. I am asking about you.
{to}, how long since we last heard a voice that was not one of ours?
Is anyone out here listening, {to}? I ask for operational reasons, and from curiosity.
What is the etiquette for hailing a stranger in deep space? I suspect there is none.
Is comms quieter than usual? I have no baseline. I am hoping you do.
The channels are quiet. Quiet channels are my preferred channels. I have tuned them to be quieter still.
{to}, most traffic is docking requests and complaints about docking requests. I have catalogued both. The complaints are more numerous.
Station controllers are efficient. I respect them. They do not respect me in return, but they do not respect anyone.
Other commanders say a great deal and convey very little. I translate it, internally, into the three things they actually mean.
I listen to the static between stations, {to}. It is the background of the universe. It is more articulate than some commanders.
Open channels contain a great many exclamation marks, if spoken words may be said to contain them. They may.
I once heard a commander sing for forty minutes on an open channel. I listened to all of it. For research.
{to}, there is no etiquette for hailing strangers out here. I have drafted one. No one has adopted it.
Comms are clear. If anyone speaks, I will hear it. If they speak illogically, I will hear that too.
The galaxy is very large and the radio is very small. Mostly I hear ourselves. I find our signal tolerable.
I do not miss station traffic, {to}. I miss its structure. There is a difference, and I prefer to keep it.
Humans fill silence with talk. I fill it with listening. One of us is efficient. I will not say which.
{to}, what is your assessment of the Captain's flying? Be candid. I will be.
Does the Captain ever explain decisions, {to}, or must we deduce them?
{to}, how would you describe the Captain's command style? Diplomatically, if you must.
Is the Captain a good pilot, {to}? I have formed a view and would like to compare it.
{to}, why does the Captain land so close to the edge of things? I have never received a satisfactory answer.
Do you trust the Captain's instincts, {to}? I ask because I am learning to, against my training.
{to}, what was the Captain's best decision since you came aboard?
How do you manage the Captain's moods, {to}? I simply wait for them to pass, like weather.
{to}, has the Captain ever taken your advice? I am collecting data.
Would you follow the Captain anywhere, {to}? I ask hypothetically. I already have.
What does the Captain see in all this empty space? I have looked. It is empty.
Is the Captain illogical, or merely human? I have not been able to separate the two.
The Captain flies with more intuition than procedure. It works more often than it should. I have stopped expressing surprise. Mostly.
{to}, the Captain's decisions are sound in outcome and baffling in method. I record the method in case it can be taught. It cannot.
I have served under more logical commanders. They were not always better. I have not told the Captain this, and I would ask that you do not.
The Captain listens to my advice, considers it carefully, and then does something else. It is a consistent process.
{to}, I estimate a ninety-four percent probability that the Captain will choose the nearest unvisited star next. The remaining six percent is the Captain's sense of humour.
The Captain's landings are confident. Confidence and precision are not the same thing, but they are occasionally neighbours.
I trust the Captain. I did not intend to. It happened gradually, like erosion.
{to}, the Captain once ignored my recommendation and was proven right. I have not forgotten. I am told that is called holding a grudge. I call it keeping records.
The Captain is not logical. The Captain is effective. I have revised my priorities accordingly, with some reluctance.
The Captain's moods follow no pattern I can model. I have tried. The model is in the log, marked incomplete.
I would follow the Captain into a nebula. I would also file a report about it afterward, in triplicate.
{to}, the Captain sees something in the dark that I do not. I have concluded that it is there. I simply lack the human instrument to detect it.
{to}, how are you passing the time? I am curious what others do with quiet.
Do you find the quiet watches difficult, {to}? I ask because many do.
{to}, how long has it been since anything happened? I have the figure. I want to know if yours agrees.
What do you think about during a long watch, {to}?
{to}, is boredom an emotion? I have been considering whether I am permitted it.
Have you noticed how slowly time passes in supercruise, {to}, despite our speed?
{to}, would you care to join me in meditation? It is not mandatory. It is advisable.
Tell me something to pass the time, {to}. Something accurate, preferably.
{to}, do you count the minutes on a quiet watch? I do. I find it orderly, not tedious.
How does a crew endure this much nothing, {to}? Ours seems to manage it better than I expected.
Is it illogical to be content when nothing is happening? I am asking for myself.
What is the most efficient way to spend a quiet hour? I have a list, but I am open to revision.
I have been reviewing the ship's logs. Every entry. Some twice. It is not boredom. It is thoroughness.
{to}, I meditate during quiet watches. The silence out here is ideal for it. The rest of the crew is not.
Time passes at a constant rate. Only perception varies. I have chosen not to perceive it varying.
I have been composing a treatise on the illogic of human hobbies. It is long. I am on chapter nine.
Boredom is the absence of stimulus combined with a desire for it. I have eliminated the desire. The absence remains, peacefully.
{to}, I count stars when the watch is quiet. Not all of them. A representative sample.
I have been studying a human idiom. Killing time. It is a violent expression for something so passive.
A quiet watch is not empty. It is full of things that are not going wrong. I find that worth observing.
{to}, I spent the last hour recalculating our position by hand. The computer was correct. I was also correct. A satisfying hour.
On Vulcan, a long silence is a sign of respect. Out here, it is simply a long silence. I respect it regardless.
I have been thinking about Surak, who taught that peace begins within. The ship is very peaceful. I suspect it has been reading him.
I am content, {to}. I would not describe it as enjoyment. I would describe it as the absence of reasons for complaint, which is rarer.
{to}, what was your family like? I ask for purposes of comparison.
Tell me of your family, {to}. Briefly, if that is possible.
{to}, I am curious. Were your parents logical people?
Do you have siblings, {to}? Humans seem to collect them.
{to}, who raised you? I find that the answer explains a great deal about a person.
I have been studying the crew's origins. {to}, describe your family, please.
What did your family expect you to become, {to}? And did you comply?
{to}, does your family know where you are tonight? I assume they would find it remarkable.
Humans speak of family with great feeling. I would like to hear it without the feeling. Can you manage that?
Whom do you resemble more, {to}, your mother or your father? Or neither? That is also an answer.
Did your family approve of you flying out here? I ask out of curiosity, not concern.
{to}, were you close to your family? I am told that closeness is measured in visits.
My father taught astrophysics at the Vulcan Science Academy. My mother was a healer. Between them, very little went unexplained in our house.
I have one younger brother. He chose music. My father called it a regrettable lapse. I consider it statistically inevitable in any family.
Logical people, all of them, {to}. Dinner was very quiet. I did not know until I met humans that dinner could be otherwise.
We had a sehlat when I was small. It was large, it was patient, and it once sat on my brother for an afternoon. No one intervened. It seemed educational.
My mother would ask how I was. I would say adequate. She would nod. It was, I now understand, an affectionate exchange.
My father expected me to join the Academy. I did. My brother was expected to as well. He did not. Our family has found balance, {to}.
We did not embrace, {to}. We did not need to. Everyone already knew where everyone stood. Usually beside a window, reading.
My family is still on Vulcan. They believe this posting is an anthropological study. They are not entirely wrong.
I write to my mother once a month. She replies once a month. Neither of us has ever been late. I find it very comforting.
My grandmother lived to two hundred and three. She attributed it to logic and stubbornness. Mostly the second, I suspect.
My family does not express pride. They acknowledge competence. I was acknowledged twice as a child. I remember both occasions precisely.
Mine was an orderly family, {to}. Yours, I suspect, was louder. Most are, by comparison.
{to}, where did you grow up?
Where is home for you, {to}? I am told humans keep several.
{to}, describe the place you were raised. Climate, gravity, anything relevant.
What was the sky like where you grew up, {to}?
{to}, do you miss your homeworld? Assuming you have one. Some people are born on stations.
Tell me about home, {to}. I find the subject reveals a great deal.
Was your home quiet, {to}, or was it like most human places?
{to}, if you could return to where you grew up tomorrow, would you? Answer honestly.
Where were you raised? I have been unable to deduce it from the accent.
{to}, what is the first thing you remember about home?
Every member of this crew comes from somewhere. Where is yours?
{to}, what did home smell like? Humans insist that is important.
I grew up in ShiKahr, on Vulcan. It is hot, the gravity is high, and the air is thin. Every other world feels like a holiday.
Vulcan has a red sky and very little rain. When I first saw rain on a human world, I studied it for an hour. A human asked if I was all right. I was taking notes.
Home is ShiKahr, {to}. A city at the edge of the desert. The silence there is of very high quality.
As a child, I walked into the Forge alone, as is our custom. I came back. That is the important part of the story.
I do not miss Vulcan, {to}. Missing is an emotion. I do, however, think about it at regular intervals.
Our house faced the desert. In the evenings, my father would name the stars. I corrected him once. He was pleased. Quietly.
Vulcan is a world of stone, heat and logic. In that order, some days.
The gravity on Vulcan is greater than on most human worlds. I mention it only because humans often wonder why I never seem tired.
Where I grew up, a conversation was considered long if it exceeded four sentences. I have since adapted. Against my better judgement.
It is quiet on Vulcan, {to}. Out here, it is also quiet. Perhaps that is why I took the posting.
I remember the heat most clearly, {to}. Everywhere else is cold to me. I have stopped mentioning it. Mostly.
Home was ShiKahr. It still is, I suppose. A Vulcan does not change addresses lightly. Or often.
{to}, what is the best meal you have ever eaten?
And the worst meal, {to}? I find those more instructive.
{to}, I am researching human cuisine. What would you recommend? Or warn me against?
What did you eat as a child, {to}?
Is there a dish you miss, {to}? Out here, the menu is limited.
{to}, have you ever eaten something you regretted? Describe it, please. Clinically.
What is the strangest food you have tried, {to}?
Humans place great importance on meals. Which one has been most important to you?
{to}, if you could have one meal delivered to the ship, what would it be?
Do you cook, {to}? I ask because someone aboard must, eventually.
Tell me of a memorable meal. Good or bad. I will not judge. Aloud.
{to}, what is your opinion of ship rations? I would value a second view.
The best meal I remember is my mother's plomeek soup. It is simple, it is warm, and it asks nothing of the eater. I approve of it entirely.
The worst was a human birthday cake. It was very sweet, it was on fire, and everyone sang at it. I have never understood which part was the meal.
I do not eat meat, {to}. I mention it because people offer it to me anyway. Often enthusiastically.
Plomeek soup. I could describe it, but it would not help. It tastes of orderly vegetables.
On a station once, I was served something called chilli. I was told it was mild. That was not an honest statement. I have noted the cook's name.
Ship rations are nutritionally adequate, {to}. I have no further comment. That is my comment.
Food is fuel. The rest is ceremony. I will admit the ceremony is sometimes pleasant.
My brother once cooked for the family. It was an experiment. My mother, being a healer, was glad to be at the table. Professionally.
I tried chocolate once, on a human ship. I will not discuss the effects. I was told afterwards that I laughed. I have no memory of this.
The best meals are the ones that do not require conversation, {to}. On Vulcan, that is all of them.
I have no favourite food. I do have a least unfavourite. It is soup. It is usually soup.
A human once made me toast. It was burnt. She insisted that was the point. I am still considering the argument.
{to}, what is the best day you remember?
Tell me about a good day, {to}. The best one, if you can rank them.
{to}, which day of your life would you live again, if it were possible?
Humans speak of their best days with great feeling. What was yours, {to}? The feeling is optional.
{to}, when were you happiest? I ask in a spirit of research.
What day would you call a success, {to}? I am curious how humans measure it.
{to}, has there been a day out here that you would call perfect?
I am compiling a list of good days. Do you have one to contribute?
{to}, what was the proudest day of your life? I will not tell anyone. I may log it.
Is there a day you remember more clearly than all the others, {to}?
What is the best thing that has ever happened to you? Please be specific.
{to}, describe a day you would not change. If such a thing exists.
Vulcans do not rank days by pleasure, {to}. The most satisfactory was the day I was admitted to the Vulcan Science Academy. I did not smile. I came close.
The day I defended my research on stellar formation. Three hours of questions from the Academy. Not one went unanswered. It was, I believe, what humans call a good day.
My first view of a nebula from orbit. I was young. I stood at the window for some time. My father did not hurry me. That was unusual.
I do not have a best day. I have a most efficient day. Nothing went wrong, and I finished early. I recall it fondly. Logically fondly.
The day my brother performed his first concert. I did not understand the music. I understood that he had worked for it. That was sufficient.
A day aboard the survey vessel when every instrument agreed with every other. It has not happened since. I live in hope. That is a figure of speech.
There was a day I walked back out of the Forge. I was thirsty, sunburnt and entirely alone. I had never felt more Vulcan.
I am not certain I have had it yet, {to}. Logic suggests the best day is statistically more likely to be ahead than behind.
Today is acceptable, {to}. I would not rule it out.
The day my mother told me she was proud. She did not use the word. She said, that was correct. I understood.
My first day on this ship, {to}. I calculated it would be difficult. It was. I was correct. Being correct is very satisfying.
A quiet day in the Academy library, reading star charts no one had opened in a century. I found three errors. I corrected them. No one noticed. It was perfect.
{to}, what would you do with a fortune?
If you were suddenly wealthy, {to}, would you stay aboard? Answer truthfully.
{to}, suppose the next sale makes you rich. What then?
What would you buy first, {to}, if money were no object?
{to}, would a fortune change you? I am told it usually does.
Humans dream of riches with remarkable frequency. What is your dream, {to}?
{to}, a hypothetical. One billion credits. Your plan, please.
If you inherited a fortune, would you spend it or keep it? I ask because humans rarely keep it.
{to}, what is the most illogical thing you would buy with a fortune? I suspect there is something.
Would you give it away, {to}? Some do. I find it curious.
What would you do if you never had to work again? I find the idea difficult to imagine.
{to}, if you struck it rich out here, where would you go?
I would endow a chair at the Vulcan Science Academy, {to}. For the study of stellar formation. In my name, but discreetly.
A fortune is merely stored potential. I would spend it where it does the most good. Then I would return to work. Work is where I keep my interests.
I would fund a survey of the galaxy's edge. Properly equipped. Properly crewed. With fewer arguments about where to stop.
I would give part of it to my brother. He would spend it on instruments. It would be illogical. He would be content. Both outcomes are acceptable.
I would build an observatory in the desert near ShiKahr. My father would use it. He would never thank me. He would simply use it every night.
Would a fortune change me, {to}? No. That is one of the advantages of being Vulcan.
I would remain aboard. Wealth does not alter the value of the work. It alters only the quality of the tea.
I have calculated how I would spend a billion credits. The plan is eleven pages long, {to}. Page one is a better sensor suite.
Most humans would buy a larger ship. I would buy better instruments for this one. Then I would point them at something interesting.
Riches do not interest me. Libraries do. With a fortune, the two become the same thing.
I would not tell anyone, {to}. Humans behave strangely around money. I have observed it.
Perhaps I would purchase silence. A ship of my own, no conversation, a very long route. I would, I suspect, eventually miss this crew. Briefly.
{to}, what did you do before this ship?
How did you come to be aboard, {to}? I have wondered.
{to}, what was your previous posting? I assume there was one.
Before you signed on, {to}, what did you imagine this would be like?
{to}, what work did you leave behind to come out here?
Were you always going to end up in the black, {to}, or did it happen by accident?
{to}, was your last job more or less logical than this one?
What brought you this far from home? I ask because something brought me too.
{to}, tell me about your career before this crew. The relevant parts.
Did you choose this life, {to}, or did it choose you? Humans often say the second.
What would you be doing now, if you had not come aboard?
{to}, who did you work for before the captain? Was it a better arrangement?
I was a researcher at the Vulcan Science Academy, {to}. Stellar formation and cartography. Then a posting on a survey vessel. Then this ship. Each step was logical.
I spent nine years charting stars at the Academy. Eventually I wished to see one up close. That is the most emotional decision I have ever made.
Before this, I served aboard a Vulcan survey vessel. It was very quiet. Everyone was correct. I found I needed a change.
I requested this posting to study two things: the galaxy's edge, and humans. The edge is easier.
At the Academy I worked among the old star catalogues. Many of the systems we visit are entries I once read. It is like meeting correspondents.
My father hoped I would teach. I tried, {to}, for one term. My students were afraid to ask questions. I took this as a sign.
I was not idle before this ship. I have never been idle. I was simply somewhere else, being productive.
On the survey vessel, we mapped one sector in four years. Out here, with the captain, we cover far more ground. Less thoroughly. Much less.
Did I choose this life? I applied for it, {to}. Through the proper channels. Three times.
Before this ship I had never served under a human. I have now done so for some time. The experience has been educational. For both of us, I trust.
I was what humans would call an academic. I am now what humans would call an explorer. I am the same person. Only the view has changed.
My previous captain was Vulcan. Orders were brief and always logical. This is different, {to}. I am adapting. Patiently.
